one_liner: Go-style coroutines and channels for C; in a third-party switch shootout it beats libco and sometimes Boost.Context.
what_it_does: libmill brings Go's concurrency model to C: go(fn(...)) launches a coroutine, chmake/chs/chr and the choose block give typed channels, and msleep/fdwait/yield block cooperatively. It also includes coroutine-aware TCP, UDP, UNIX-socket, SSL, file (mfopen) and mfork wrappers. It is a single-threaded scheduler with its own API, and the same author wrote libdill as its successor.
how_it_is_fast: On x86-64 the switch is an inline-assembly setjmp/longjmp pair that saves callee-saved registers plus rdi/rsi, with no signal mask. The go() macro relocates the stack pointer onto a heap stack inside the caller's frame with a VLA filler, so a launch costs no trampoline call. goprepare() preallocates and caches stacks (default about 256 KiB) to keep allocation out of the hot path. Other architectures fall back to sigsetjmp/siglongjmp.
when_to_use: Single-threaded x86-64 C programs, such as small network daemons, written in Go-style CSP with channels and choose.
Cases where a ping-pong between two coroutines dominates; on LinuxMint x86-64 it switched faster than boost and libco in benchbox.
Existing libmill codebases that work and do not need threads or the libdill bundle model.
when_not_to_use: New projects: libdill supersedes it, the last commit was 2021-02-09, and issue #196 asks for deprecation in favour of libdill.
Many concurrent coroutines: in the 1000-coroutine benchbox runs it was slower than boost on both Linux VMs (1014 vs 894 ms, 2031 vs 1021 ms), and tbox beat it in every row.
32-bit x86: on ArchLinux i386 it was slower than boost (689 vs 485 ms for 2 coroutines), since the assembly path is x86-64 only.
Multithreaded schedulers: there is no thread support; parallelism is via mfork processes.

Modern toolchains without patching: open reports include a dns.h build failure (#188), C99 'implicit declaration of asm' (#187), GCC 6.2.1 breakage (#167), an osx segfault (#189) and a tcpconnect timeout socket leak (#181).

integration.min_toolchain: GCC or Clang with GNU C extensions (statement expressions, inline asm); autotools build
integration.platforms: x86-64 assembly switch; other POSIX via sigsetjmp fallback; epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD/macOS, poll fallback; no Windows
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe; one global scheduler per process (mfork for multi-process)

gotchas: Coroutine functions must be marked 'coroutine' (noinline), and the go() argument is evaluated on the new stack, so complex expressions in go(...) run inside the coroutine.
The x86-64 asm macros must list ymm registers as clobbered when __AVX__ is defined. Code compiled with and without AVX in one program relies on that conditional.
Its documentation was on libmill.org, which is parked (#195); the README carries no API docs or performance numbers.
The repo publishes no benchmarks; the only numbers come from the tbox author's benchbox wiki, run in VMs with no compiler flags or CPU model.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely: prefer libdill (same author, structured cancellation, per-thread contexts), or tbox, which beat libmill in every benchbox row. libmill makes sense only when you want the literal Go API surface in single-threaded C, or are already using it.
verified_claims_summary: In tboox/benchbox's switch test (10M switches), with 2 coroutines libmill took 145 ms vs boost 199 ms and libco 687 ms on a LinuxMint x86-64 VM, and 525 vs 728 ms against boost on macOS x86-64. It lost to boost on an ArchLinux i386 VM (689 vs 485 ms) and in both 1000-coroutine Linux runs, while staying ahead of libco. Compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated.
status_note: Abandoned since 2021-02-09 and effectively superseded by libdill; MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but expect to patch build errors on current GCC/Clang.
